questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14095328/assets/c8779f79dfa4964a94ace01d29f18a6c19bc08af804171ed2e2030a2401f3576.png)

The diagram above shows an enclosure built inside a pond. The velocity field of the water surface currents in the pond is given by $F(x,y)=⟨3x{y}^{2},\,-{y}^{3}⟩.$

Current part:

$\text{div}\,F\,=$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{y}^{2}+(-3{y}^{2}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{3})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x{y}^{2}) \\  & =0-(3x\cdot 2y) \\  & =-6xy.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}{{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Scalar curl of }F}\,\text{d}A.
$$

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}{{(3x{y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{P}\,dx+{{(-{y}^{3})}_{⏟}}_{Q}\,dy
$$

In part 2, we found that the scalar curl of $F$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-6xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A={∬}_{D}-6xy\,\text{d}A.
$$

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-6xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}-6(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

                            The net $L$ is represented by the line segment shown in the diagram above. 
Calculate the flux of $F$ through $L,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n.$

questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

* the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

* the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the line segment $L,$ we have

$$
x=\sqrt{2}t,\,y=-\sqrt{2}t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the line from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x{y}^{2} \\  & =3(\sqrt{2}t)(-\sqrt{2}t)^{2} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}, \\ Q(x,y) & =-{y}^{3} \\  & =-(-\sqrt{2}t)^{3} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}t)=\sqrt{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{2}t)=-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{L}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{L}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (-\sqrt{2})-(2\sqrt{2}{t}^{3})\cdot (\sqrt{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-12{t}^{3}-4{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-16{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4[{t}^{4}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4(1-0) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

As we saw earlier, we can use Green's theorem to write our line integral in polar coordinates as 

$$
{∮}_{∂R}3x{y}^{2}\,dx-{y}^{3}\,dy={∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta .
$$

But this time, our region $R$ (in polar coordinates) is given by 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{Δ}-3{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r \\  & =-3{[\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{-2}]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}]}_{r=1}^{r=2}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(1-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}({2}^{4}-{1}^{4}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
